newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan car makers seen facing stiff competition.
newsitem.headline: Japan car makers seen facing stiff competition.

text.p: Japan's car makers have set rosy targets for 1997, but industry analysts say that just means a fierce sales battle compounded by a feeble economic recovery and an expected curb in exports.
Japan's top five car makers earlier this month predicted increased domestic production and sales in 1997 over 1996, mainly due to the introduction of new models.

The five makers -- Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor, Honda Motor, Mitsubishi Motors and Mazda Motor -- said they expected sales to increase by 3.7 percent to 7.8 percent, figures which industry analysts say are too high.
"They are too optimistic. It is impossible for them to reach those targets," Noriyuki Matsushima, a senior analyst with Nikko Research, said.
Analysts said car makers publicly announced seemingly impossible sales targets to force dealers to try hard to boost sales.
Toyota expects growth of four percent in 1997 domestic sales, Nissan 3.7 percent. Honda 5.5 percent, Mitsubishi 5.0 percent rise and Mazda 7.8 percent.
Analysts said the car makers knew that reaching those predictions would not be easy.
"Makers will face a stiff battle and those who can give more incentives to dealers will win the war," Matsushima said.
Analysts said the sales battle would be more intense than usual because of tight consumer spending due to Japan's slow economic recovery and an expected hesitancy to rely on exports.
"Japan will have to curb its vehicle exports in the second half of next year to avoid a possible revival of trade friction with the United States," Matsushima said.
Car exports have boomed in the last six months, leading to worries about increased trade problems with the United States.

Early in November, the American Automobile Manufacturers Association warned Japan about that after Japan announced a more than 30 percent jump in its trade surplus with the United States, due mainly to a rebound in vehicle exports powered by a weaker yen.
The yen stood at around 114 to the dollar on Friday, compared with about 100 a year ago. The cheaper yen makes Japanese products more competitive in overseas markets.
The analysts said that meant the car makers would have to fight it out in the domestic market, with price discounts and new models, if they hoped to boost sales.
But a planned rise in Japan's consumption tax to five precent from the current three percent from April 1 is expected to hurt sales, as are general worries about the state of the economy.
The government has forecast gross domestic product growth of just 1.9 percent for the fiscal year which begins on April first, its lowest prediction ever.
Analysts said the likely result of the sales battle would be a widening of the sales gap among Japanese car makers in 1997 with top maker Toyota the winner.

"Toyota should handsomely boost its profits next year, helped by cost-cutting, caused by the effects of larger output (pushed up by robust sales)," said Nobuaki Yanachi, senior analyst with Kankaku Research.
He said Toyota had a wider range of new models and the financial strength to allow it to provide sufficient attractive incentives to dealers.
Honda's profits should continue to grow next year, but at a slower rate because of rising sales costs, Yanachi said.
Mitsubishi and Mazda were likely to face a harder time in 1997 due to the harsh competition, Yanachi said, while Nissan's performance would depend on how its new models fare.
